title: IP over Avian Carriers with Quality of Service

hero.subtitle: Extending IP over Avian Carriers with Quality of Service mechanisms

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This memo amends RFC 1149, the 1990 April Fools' standard for carrying IP datagrams on avian carriers, with Quality of Service information. It is a follow-up joke RFC that borrows real networking vocabulary (queueing, MPLS, NAT, multicast, MIBs) and applies it to birds. The RFC's own abstract calls the result "an experimental, not recommended standard".

Published on 1 April 1999, nine years after RFC 1149. The document labels itself Experimental (the RFC Editor index now lists it as Informational), and it updates RFC 1149.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 2549 is an April Fools' memo, published on 1 April 1999, that adds quality of service to RFC 1149, which describes carrying IP datagrams on birds. It applies real networking terms such as queueing, MPLS, NAT and MIBs to birds. Its abstract calls the result "an experimental, not recommended standard."

sections.title: Improvements over RFC 1149
sections.content:
RFC 1149 carried datagrams but had no notion of service levels. RFC 2549 adds four service levels, a way to mark and queue carriers, and two security classes.

Service levels
Concorde, First, Business and Coach. Concorde class offers expedited data delivery, and Concorde and First earn 50% bonus frequent flyer miles per packet.
Marking and queueing
The level is marked per carrier by bar-code on the wing. A reader scans each carrier as it enters the router and enqueues it in the proper queue, gated to prevent exit until the proper time. Carriers may sleep while enqueued.
Secure classes
For secure networks, carriers may be Prime or Choice. Prime carriers are self-keying when using public key encryption; some distributors falsely classify Choice carriers as Prime.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1149 had no service levels. This memo adds four: Concorde, First, Business and Coach, marked by bar-code on each carrier's wing. A reader scans each carrier on entry and places it in the right queue. For secure networks it adds two classes, Prime and Choice. The memo notes that some distributors falsely classify Choice carriers as Prime.

sections.title: Quality of Service
sections.content:
The memo borrows queueing terms from real routers. Weighted fair queueing (WFQ) MAY be implemented using scales, and packets MAY be marked for deletion using RED paint while enqueued. Round-robin queueing is not recommended: robins make for well-tuned networks but do not support the necessary auto-homing feature. Ostriches are an alternate carrier with much greater bulk transfer capability but slower delivery, and they require bridges between domains.

Carriers in the queue too long may leave log entries, as shown on the scale in the RFC's ASCII drawing.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo borrows queueing terms from real routers and applies them to birds. Weighted fair queueing may be done with scales, and packets may be marked for deletion with red paint. It advises against round-robin queueing. Ostriches are an alternate carrier with greater capacity but slower delivery.

sections.title: MIB and Security
sections.content:
RFC 2549 includes a mock SNMP MIB. AvCarrier2 defines the carrier as a taxonomic path down to Columba livia, and PulseRate is a read-only gauge of the carrier's pulse "as measured in neck". The carriers will not line up in lexicographic order but will naturally order in a large V shape, and bulk retrieval uses the Powerful Get-Net operator.

The Security Considerations say there are privacy issues with stool pigeons and that agoraphobic carriers are very insecure in operation. The Patent Considerations note ongoing litigation about which is the prior art: carrier or egg.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo includes a mock SNMP MIB that defines the carrier as a taxonomic path down to Columba livia and a read-only pulse rate. The security section jokes about privacy issues with stool pigeons and insecure agoraphobic carriers. The patent section jokes about a dispute over which came first, the carrier or the egg.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Routing
sections.content:
RFC 2549 does not define a frame layout. Instead it jokes about how familiar networking techniques fare with birds. Encapsulation may be done with saran wrappers, though unintentional encapsulation in hawks has been known to occur, with decapsulation being messy and the packets mangled. Carriers normally bypass bridges and tunnels but will seek out worm hole tunnels, and they may be confused by mirrors.

The carriers have an average TTL of 15 years, so their use in expanding ring searches is limited. Multicasting is supported but requires a clone device, and carriers may be lost if they are based on a tree as it is being pruned.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo defines no frame layout and instead jokes about how familiar techniques fare with birds. Encapsulation may use saran wrap. Carriers usually bypass bridges and tunnels, have an average TTL of 15 years, and need a clone device for multicasting.

subtitle: Extending IP over Avian Carriers with Quality of Service mechanisms
summary: RFC 2549 amends the 1990 April Fools' RFC 1149 on IP over pigeons by adding quality of service. Carriers get a service level (Concorde, First, Business or Coach) marked as a bar-code on the wing, are scanned and queued at the router, and the memo goes on to joke about NATs, MPLS, multicast and a bird MIB. It calls itself "an experimental, not recommended standard".

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2549 is an April Fools' memo that amends RFC 1149, IP over pigeons, by adding quality of service. Carriers receive a service level marked by bar-code on the wing and are queued at the router. It also jokes about NATs, MPLS, multicast and a bird MIB, and calls itself "an experimental, not recommended standard."

tldr.problem: RFC 1149 carried IP datagrams on pigeons but gave no way to treat some of them better than others.
tldr.mechanism: Each carrier is marked with a service level by a bar-code on the wing; a reader scans it as it enters the router and enqueues it in the matching queue, gated until the proper time.
tldr.outcome: A joke Experimental RFC that mirrors real queueing, NAT and MPLS arguments; it is not meant to be deployed.

today: Nobody deploys this, and the RFC says so. It lives on as a classic of the April Fools' RFC tradition, which also produced RFC 6214, an adaptation of RFC 1149 for IPv6. RFC 1149 itself was implemented in earnest in 2001 by the Bergen Linux User Group, which sent real pings by pigeon.
